title: Index Funds Explained: Why Boring Investing Wins
description:
Most professional fund managers lose to a simple index fund over the long run. In this video I explain index funds from three angles: the numbers (fees, diversification, why the pros lose and Buffett's million dollar bet), the psychology that makes boring investing so hard, and a step by step playbook to start in one afternoon.

Get The Ryan Rover Money Playbook: [LINK HERE]

0:00 Intro
1:48 How we got the numbers
2:16 Angle 1: The Numbers
2:24 1. What an index fund is
3:54 2. Bogle's folly
5:16 3. Costs are everything
6:36 4. Why the pros lose
7:46 5. Diversification for free
8:58 6. Taxes and turnover
10:03 7. The market's long run
11:24 Angle 2: The Psychology
11:45 8. The excitement trap
12:46 9. Overconfidence
13:51 10. The behavior gap
15:15 11. Headlines and noise
16:12 12. Fear of missing out
17:11 13. Average is extraordinary
18:12 14. The power of not deciding
19:27 Angle 3: The Playbook
19:38 15. Pick the right account
20:46 16. Choose simple funds
21:46 17. Automate it
22:34 18. Rebalance once a year
23:26 19. Stay the course
24:15 20. Let time do the work
25:12 Getting started in one afternoon
26:40 Index funds at every age
27:31 The million dollar bet
28:41 Questions people ask
31:20 Four index fund mistakes
32:50 Recap
33:24 What to do next

Sources:
- S&P Dow Jones Indices, SPIVA U.S. Scorecards and Persistence Scorecards
- Investment Company Institute, Investment Company Fact Book: expense ratios of index and active equity funds
- Morningstar: U.S. passive fund assets overtaking active (early 2024)
- Morningstar, Mind the Gap: investor returns vs fund returns
- John C. Bogle, The Little Book of Common Sense Investing; Vanguard history (1975, first index fund 1976)
- Warren Buffett, Berkshire Hathaway shareholder letters (2013 instructions; 2017 bet results)
- Barber and Odean, Trading Is Hazardous to Your Wealth (Journal of Finance, 2000)
- Hendrik Bessembinder, Do Stocks Outperform Treasury Bills? (Journal of Financial Economics, 2018)
- IRS, IRA and Roth IRA rules and limits
- Growth examples: monthly compounding at stated average yearly returns (illustrations, not promises)
